headline: Bunker Pods Round the Hook: Bluefish Blitzes and Channel-Edge Fluke Carry the Bay
subhead: With stripers thinned by summer heat, Raritan Bay's action has shifted to bluefish on bunker and fluke working the drop-offs off Flynn's Knoll and Romer Shoal.
body_markdown:
_AI fishing-intelligence report. It was prepared from 0 supplied evidence records and 17 supplied analysis inputs; it does not claim firsthand fishing._

If I'm putting a boat in the water this week, I'm running to Flynn's Knoll first thing and working the last two hours of the incoming, because that's where the bunker have been stacking and that's where the blitzes are breaking. Early August in this bay isn't a striper month — anybody telling you different is selling you something — but it's a bluefish month, and right now the bluefish are exactly where they're supposed to be: parked under bait.

We flagged this pattern two weeks back — said bunker schools pushing north out of the Belmar blitz zone would round Sandy Hook and pull predators in behind them within a day or two of entering the bay. That's precisely what's been playing out. The pods have worked their way up past the Hook and into the bay proper, holding thick off Keyport and along the edge of Flynn's Knoll, and the bluefish have followed them in exactly the way that pattern predicted. What surprised me a little is how quiet the striper end of that equation has stayed — the blues showed up hard, the bass mostly didn't. That's the story of this bay in the heat of summer: warm surface water pushes the linesiders down and out, but bluefish don't care one bit, and bunker-fed blitzes are still blitzes.

The topwater window is short and it's tide-driven. Dawn on the last of the outgoing at the Knoll, or the top of the incoming pushing bait up against Romer Shoal — those are the two windows worth building a morning around. When the birds start working and the bunker start showering, throw a Hopkins or a Kastmaster in the 1.5 to 2-ounce range, silver or bunker-pattern, and don't finesse it — long cast, let it sink a beat, then rip it back through the fray. Poppers work too when the blitz stays on top, but once the bluefish push the bunker down a few feet, the metal outproduces everything else because it gets through the strike zone faster. Fish are running mixed sizes — plenty of harbor blues in the 2 to 4-pound class mixed with better fish pushing 6 to 8 pounds, and when you find the right pod those numbers can be aggressive fast fishing, though it's patchy: some mornings the blitz never fully materializes and you're left picking at stragglers on bunker chunks instead.

While the blues own the surface, the channel-edge fluke program is still the more consistent producer if you want dinner. The drop-offs along Flynn's Knoll, the deeper cuts running off Romer Shoal, and the edges of the Keyport Flats channel are all holding fish in that 18 to 30-foot range, and the pattern hasn't changed from what's worked all summer: white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4 to 1-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom on the drift, tight to where the sand breaks into mud. Best window is the last two hours of the outgoing into dead low, when the current slows enough to hold bottom contact without needing to overweight. Sizes have been mixed — a fair number of shorts mixed with keepers to 20 inches, occasional better fish pushing 22 to 24 off the deeper edges near Romer. It's not a doormat month, but it's a keep-you-busy month, and busy beats slow.

Weakfish have thinned out the way they always do once the calendar flips into August — a few incidental fish still turning up on the fluke drift, nothing worth building a trip around. Porgies are the quiet win right now: working the structure inside the Reach and around the bay-side rockpiles with sandworms or clam on a simple high-low rig is producing steady, if unglamorous, action, and it's a good option for anyone who wants a full cooler without fighting current and boat traffic for bunker pods. Blackfish are off the table entirely — season's closed in these waters until fall, so don't waste bait on the tog grounds yet.

Wind and heat are the two variables worth watching heading into next week. If the bay stays under this stable high-pressure pattern, expect the bunker to keep holding tight around the Hook and Flynn's Knoll rather than scattering, which should keep the bluefish blitzes reliable through the week — that's the same stable-weather logic that's kept this bite alive since it started building. If a front pushes through and stirs the surface, the blitzes will scatter with the bait and you'll need to hunt harder, likely pushing deeper into the channels off Keyport where the bunker tend to regroup. My move for the week: mornings on the blitz at the Knoll or Romer Shoal while the window holds, then sliding into the channel edges on the outgoing for fluke once the topwater shuts down. It's not a striper week in this bay — but bluefish and fluke are giving up enough to make the trip worth the gas.
